facts.fact: Caridina babaulti was described by Bouvier in 1918.
The type material was collected in British India by Guy Babault in 1913–1914, and a lectotype is held at the Paris museum (MNHN).
The type locality is Majghaon in Madhya Pradesh, central India. Labels on the type specimens also name Masegaon in Maharashtra.
It belongs to the genus Caridina in the family Atyidae.
In 2019 Pandya and Richard redescribed it from the type specimens and from new material collected in the Shetrunji River. In the same paper they described the related species Caridina kutchi.
The rostrum is as long as the antennular peduncle or shorter, 0.4–0.7 times the carapace length, with 14–25 teeth.
It has a long, serrated rostrum and stripes, and some individuals have orange eyes with a visible pupil.
It can change colour with lighting, substrate, breeding season, age, or when startled, ranging from red and orange through brown, green and yellow to almost steel blue.
In the trade it comes in green and zebra forms. The zebra form is light brown with dark vertical stripes, and green individuals may turn orange or brown when stressed.
Shops often sell it as Caridina cf. babaulti because its identity is not settled.
It is native to inland waters of central, western and southern India.
It has been confirmed from the Shetrunji River on the Saurashtra Peninsula in Gujarat.
In 2021 it was recorded in Europe's open waters for the first time, at Miskolctapolca, Hungary, where 7 of 120 non-native shrimps collected were this species.
Shop sources say the green and zebra forms live in small, clear Indian rivers with slow flow, dense plants and rocky bottoms.
It is sold in the aquarium trade, most often in its green form.
Its presence in Hungary is most likely due to aquarium owners releasing it. If not removed, it might form a viable population.
A hobbyist reports that it ships poorly, with high losses in transit, and suggests buying it from a store or breeder.
A hobbyist reports that it is rare in the hobby.
A German shop sells shrimp labelled Caridina cf. babaulti and gives their origin as India.
A hobbyist suggests starting from about 20 litres (5 gallons), as an established, planted tank.
One shop gives a minimum of 20 litres for a small group.
A hobbyist keeps it at 24 °C and pH 7.4 and stresses stable water over big swings.
According to a hobbyist, it needs the same conditions as Neocaridina cherry shrimp, and soft water is not required.
It is mainly a grazer of biofilm, algae and microorganisms, and it should not be overfed.
It is omnivorous and accepts shrimp food, flakes, algae tablets, blanched vegetables, and a little frozen food such as Daphnia.
A hobbyist gives cuttlefish bone as a calcium supplement.
According to a hobbyist, it is timid, likes to hide, and gathers in groups more than cherry shrimp do.
A hobbyist says it is safe only with very few fish, such as Otocinclus.
A shop describes it as shyer than many dwarf shrimp, needing plenty of hiding places, and says most fish will eat it.
Telling the sexes apart is harder than in cherry shrimp. Females have a wider abdomen (skirt) for carrying eggs.
In aquaria, females carry about 30–50 eggs for about 30 days, according to a hobbyist.
In aquaria, the young are tiny, grow and colour up slowly, and seem to survive in lower numbers than cherry shrimp, according to a hobbyist.
An ovigerous female was among the shrimps collected in the wild in Hungary.
A shop says it breeds more slowly than Neocaridina, at a rate closer to bee shrimp.

care.quote: about an inch and a half maximum
Keep the water temperature between 22 to 26°C (72 to 79°F).
